name: Ryegrass
model: written by hand (Claude) from the Urdu KB

aspects.overview: Ryegrass is a very useful multi-cut winter fodder. It keeps growing in severe cold and frost, can be grown on saline (kallar) land, and makes very good hay. It tolerates hard cold but not much heat; it suits areas with irrigation or high rainfall. Main rabi fodders are berseem, lucerne, oats and ryegrass; berseem is often sown mixed with oats, mustard or ryegrass, which gives an earlier first cut and more fodder. Yield: 600 to 700 maunds of green fodder per acre alone, 900 to 1,000 maunds mixed with berseem; seed yield up to 2.5 maunds per acre. Demand is rising with the need for more milk and meat.
aspects.varieties: Approved variety: RG-1, developed by the Fodder Research Institute Sargodha. Ryegrass Supreme is less affected by stem rot. Use clean, healthy, weed-free seed; market seed often contains shaftal, chicory (kasni), riwari and onion-weed seed. If chicory is mixed in, soak seed in a 5 percent salt solution, remove the floating chicory seed, then wash the seed well before sowing. Seed is available from the Punjab Seed Corporation, the Fodder Research Institute Sargodha, the Regional Agricultural Research Institute Bahawalpur and the Fodder Research Station Faisalabad.
aspects.sowing:
Soil: heavy loam is best. Prepare the land with one turn of a soil-turning (mouldboard) plough, then four ploughings with planking, until the soil is fine.
Time: October or November.
Seed rate: 6 to 8 kg per acre of clean seed, broadcast in soil at workable moisture (wattar), then a light planking. Drilling in lines one foot apart gives good results.
Mixed with berseem: in standing water broadcast berseem first, then ryegrass. Seed rate for the mix: 7 kg berseem and 1 kg ryegrass per acre. (Berseem with oats: 6 kg berseem and 8 to 10 kg oats; with mustard: 8 kg berseem and 1 to 2 kg mustard.)
Rotate ryegrass with other rabi crops.
aspects.fertilizer: Needs 32 kg nitrogen and 25 kg phosphorus per acre. At sowing apply 2.5 bags SSP plus half a bag of urea, or 1 bag DAP. Give 1 bag of urea with the first irrigation. If stem rot appears, cut back nitrogen; use potash and don't overuse nitrogen.
aspects.irrigation: Usually 3 to 4 irrigations. First irrigation three weeks after sowing, then as needed. In the seed crop, water as needed during flowering and pollination. Avoid over-watering (stem rot) and don't let water from a diseased field reach healthy ones.
aspects.pests_diseases:
Rule: never spray the crop meant for fodder. Spray only seed crops, or spray after cutting the fodder, in the morning or evening to protect bees. Nothing should be sprayed 20 to 25 days before cutting.
Armyworm (lashkari sundi): greenish-brown caterpillar with yellow stripes and two black spots behind the head; curls up when touched. From February–March it eats leaves down to the veins, plus flowers and buds. Don't spray full-grown caterpillars; wait until they pupate. Keep the crop weed-free, use light and sex-pheromone traps, and dig water-filled trenches with kerosene around badly hit fields so caterpillars can't move on. In severe attack, after cutting, spray per acre 50 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml lufenuron.
American bollworm: eats leaves; hay crops suffer most. If essential, cut the fodder and then spray per acre 40 ml spinosad, or 25 ml flubendiamide, or 40 to 50 ml chlorantraniliprole, or 200 ml emamectin benzoate, or 200 ml lufenuron. Use light and pheromone traps; check seed crops and spray while caterpillars are young.
Looper (kubri sundi): green caterpillar that loops when moving; webs and eats tender leaves. Same rules: don't spray fodder, spray after cutting; trenches with kerosene around fields.
Whitefly (seed crop): sucks sap, leaves turn yellow with black sooty mould. Spray per acre 250 ml acetamiprid, or 400 ml flonicamid, or 500 ml pyriproxyfen.
Thrips (seed crop): suck sap so leaves dry. Spray 200 ml chlorfenapyr per acre, and use yellow or blue sticky traps.
Aphid (sust tela): dark green, sucks sap, sooty mould follows. Sow treated seed; never spray the fodder crop. On the seed crop spray per acre 200 ml imidacloprid or nitenpyram, or 250 ml acetamiprid or bifenthrin.
Shoot fly: enters and dries the shoots; in severe attack cut the fodder, then spray 200 ml imidacloprid or emamectin benzoate per acre.
Fodder weevil: larva and adult eat green leaf tissue and new shoots; cut the fodder early. On the seed crop spray 40 to 50 ml flubendiamide or chlorantraniliprole per acre.
Lygus and sting bugs: damage buds, flowers and green pods so flowers drop and seed shrivels, mostly in the seed crop. Spray a recommended insecticide.
Stem rot: use a lower seed rate, avoid over-watering, keep water from diseased fields away from healthy ones, rotate crops, use potash and don't overuse nitrogen. Ryegrass Supreme is less affected.
aspects.weeds:
No weedicide is sprayed on the fodder crop: any weeds are cut with the fodder and fed to animals. Frequent cutting also controls weeds, so rotate with other rabi crops.
Itsit: spray pendimethalin 1.5 litres per acre three weeks to a month before sowing and irrigate; plough at wattar and leave open.
Note: grass-killer sprays (such as quizalofop) are not for ryegrass, because ryegrass is itself a grass.
Do not hoe right after spraying: dust can carry the chemical into the farmer's body.
aspects.harvesting: Fodder: first cut 60 days after sowing, later cuts every 45 to 50 days. Seed crop: cut a little before full maturity, because seed starts shedding on the ground long before it is fully ripe. No spray of any kind 20 to 25 days before cutting.
aspects.other: Ryegrass can be grown on saline (kallar) land and in cold, frosty areas; it is often sown mixed with berseem.

timing.harvesting: first cut 60 days after sowing, then every 45 to 50 days
